name: Stock
summary: Matthiola incana is the accepted species commonly called stock. Many commercial stock varieties are hybrids involving other Matthiola species, so this profile does not imply a particular color or cultivar.

identity.short: Accepted species; commercial series may be interspecific hybrids
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Matthiola incana. NC State notes that many stock varieties are hybrids involving M. incana, M. sinuata and M. odorata; the common name alone does not identify a hybrid or named variety.

growth.guidance: NC State describes stock as upright, generally grown as an annual or biennial in its regional context, with fragrant flowers and a reported height up to 3 feet. Heat above about 80°F can shorten performance; this is not cultivar-specific.

cultivation.short: Cool conditions, full sun and consistently moist drainage
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and humusy soil that remains consistently moist but drains well, and notes tolerance of light shade. It reports decline during summer heat above 80°F and poor performance in hot nights; regional season timing should be adapted locally.

propagation.short: Seed sowing is documented; hybrid identity may vary
propagation.guidance: NC State supports direct sowing or indoor starts 6–8 weeks before the last frost and successive sowings at two-week intervals. It warns that many commercial varieties are interspecific hybrids; this species record does not promise seed-grown offspring match a named packet variety.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Garden-soil guidance does not establish hydroponic compatibility.

evidence.note: NC State describes stock as upright; commercial stock hybrids are not assigned this identity.

height.reason: The source's broad maximum is not selected as a cultivar-independent mature height.

spacing.reason: Outdoor border spacing is not indoor-system pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not mapped to indoor grow-light intensity.

name: Four-o'clock
summary: Mirabilis jalapa is a fragrant, late-day flowering species known as four-o'clock or marvel-of-Peru. Flowers vary in color; no cultivar or color form is assigned.

identity.short: Accepted species; flower color is not a cultivar identity
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Mirabilis jalapa, native from Mexico to Nicaragua. NC State notes flowers in multiple colors and patterns, so the generic identity does not specify one color or named cultivar.

growth.short: Branching perennial in warm climates; often seasonal elsewhere
growth.guidance: NC State describes a semi-woody perennial in warmer gardens, grown as an annual in colder regional areas. Its fragrant trumpet-shaped blooms open late in the day; tuberous roots can regrow or be stored in some climates.

cultivation.short: Full sun preferred; moist, drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State says the species tolerates most soils and partial shade but prefers full sun and moist, occasionally wet, humus-rich soil that drains. Regional tuber overwintering depends on climate and is not a universal annual-care rule.

propagation.short: Seed and division are documented routes
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed and division. It says soaking seeds overnight can speed germination but gives no depth, temperature or duration; old plants may form tuberous roots. Do not treat this as a named-cultivar fidelity guarantee.

safety.guidance: NC State reports low-severity poison characteristics, especially for roots and seeds, and possible skin irritation when handling roots.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor soil culture does not establish hydroponic compatibility.

evidence.note: NC State describes the species as erect and multi-stemmed.

spacing.reason: Garden-bed spacing is not indoor-system pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Common Morning Glory
summary: Ipomoea purpurea is a fast-growing annual twining vine with morning-opening flowers. It is distinct from sweet potato and moonflower, which belong to other Ipomoea identities.

identity.short: Accepted species within a diverse genus
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ipomoea purpurea. The genus also includes sweet potato and moonflower; this record is limited to common morning glory and does not identify a named flower-color cultivar.

growth.short: Twining annual vine with morning flowers
growth.guidance: NC State describes a rapidly climbing annual vine, often 6–10 ft tall and 3–6 ft wide in one season. Flowers open in the morning and close later; dimensions are species-level garden context, not a selected cultivar guarantee.

cultivation.short: Full sun and moist, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and moderately fertile, moist but well-drained soil. It may need pruning to control its vigorous climbing size; provide support where grown vertically. The source discusses outdoor cultivation, not indoor hydroponics.

propagation.short: Seed propagation; manage self-seeding and local spread
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed propagation and notes the species can reseed readily and is invasive in some places. Its genus-level guide describes nicking a hard seed coat and soaking overnight; that pretreatment remains genus-scope, not a measured I. purpurea protocol.

safety.guidance: NC State flags low-severity poison characteristics and notes that large amounts of seeds may cause symptoms.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor vine cultivation does not establish indoor hydroponic compatibility.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility vocabulary has no climbing/twining value; the supported habit remains described in the Plant Profile.

height.reason: Outdoor vine height is not adopted as an indoor-system dimension.

spread.reason: Broad outdoor vine spread is not an indoor-system dimension.

spacing.reason: Outdoor trellis spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Full sun outdoors is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Garden Impatiens
summary: Impatiens walleriana is a popular shade-flowering species often grown as an annual outside tropical climates. This species-level profile does not identify a particular color, series or disease-resistance cultivar.

identity.short: Accepted species; named series and colors unspecified
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Impatiens walleriana and lists older names including I. holstii and I. sultanii as synonyms. NC State describes extensive cultivar variation; no particular cultivar is implied.

growth.short: Fast-growing, dense or mounding flowering plant
growth.guidance: NC State describes the species as a tropical perennial often grown as an annual in temperate gardens, typically 0.5–2 ft tall and similarly wide. Bloom timing is regional; no named-series guarantee is implied.

cultivation.short: Part shade to shade; moist but not waterlogged
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends part to full shade and moist, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter. Heat and dry spells can cause wilting; overwatering can cause rot. Outdoor/container guidance does not establish hydroponic suitability.

maintenance.short: Trim leggy growth to refresh appearance
maintenance.guidance: NC State suggests trimming about the top third in late summer when plants become leggy. Disease resistance varies among cultivars; the species profile does not claim it.

propagation.short: Seed and stem cuttings are documented
propagation.guidance: NC State documents seed collection from ripe capsules, indoor sowing in late winter and stem cuttings. Seed-grown plants may take several months to flower and should go outdoors after the last spring frost; no numeric germination temperature or depth is provided.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Shade-garden and potting-medium guidance does not prove recirculating hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: NC State describes dense mounding and clumping forms across species-level garden culture.

height.reason: The reported range includes cultivar-dependent forms and is not selected as a universal mature size.

spacing.reason: Bedding-plant spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Shade exposure outdoors is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Cardinal Flower
summary: Lobelia cardinalis is a moisture-loving North American perennial with vivid red flower spikes that attract hummingbirds and butterflies. It is distinct from other Lobelia species and the named cultivar Queen Victoria.

identity.short: Accepted species; cultivar Queen Victoria excluded
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Lobelia cardinalis. NC State mentions several cultivars, including Queen Victoria; this profile does not attribute that cultivar's bronze foliage or other traits to the species.

growth.short: Tall herbaceous perennial with red flower spikes
growth.guidance: NC State reports plants around 4–5 ft tall and 1–2 ft wide in its regional garden context, with blooms from late summer into mid-fall. These are species-level dimensions; cultivars may differ.

cultivation.short: Keep soil consistently moist; part shade to sun
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends rich, medium-to-wet soil that should not dry, with part shade to full sun and afternoon shade appreciated in hot summers. It tolerates brief flooding and suits wet meadows, woodland shade, streamsides and rain gardens; this does not establish hydroponic compatibility.

propagation.short: Seed or spring rosette separation are documented
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed propagation and spring separation of rosettes from the parent. The selected page gives no home sowing or germination protocol; do not borrow details from another Lobelia species.

safety.short: NC State reports medium-severity toxicity if large quantities are eaten
safety.guidance: NC State lists toxicity for ingestion of plant parts including leaves, flowers, roots, seeds and sap. The warning concerns ingestion, not ordinary contact.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Wet-soil and rain-garden tolerance does not establish nutrient-solution compatibility.

evidence.note: NC State describes erect flowering spikes and upright stalks.

height.reason: A species-level outdoor range is not used as a universal indoor size.

spread.reason: The regional garden width is not an indoor-system spread.

spacing.reason: Outdoor garden spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor sun/shade exposure is not an indoor grow-light tier.
